courses.title: Help Desk Essentials
courses.description: The non-technical core of great support: communication, professionalism, documentation, and the ticket process.

content.intro: What Tier-1 support really is, and what good looks like on day one.

p: Help desk is the first line of IT support: you receive issues, triage them, resolve what you can, and escalate the rest — while keeping users informed.

note.text: In the real world: Employers hire for attitude and communication as much as technical skill — a calm, clear tech who documents well beats a silent genius on the phones.

content.practice: In your own words, describe the difference between Tier 1 and Tier 2.

o: the first human contact for common issues

quiz.p: Issues beyond your scope should be…

quiz.ex: Soft skills matter as much as technical.

content.intro: How you talk to users determines their experience as much as the fix does.

ul: Listen fully, then confirm the problem back
Avoid jargon; explain in the user's terms
Set expectations (what you'll do, how long)
Focus on the next action, not blame
Follow up when you promise to

note.text: In the real world: A user whose issue takes a day but who is kept informed is happier than one fixed in an hour with silence — communication is the product.

p: Be warm, concise, and confident. Written tickets: clear subject, plain steps, no jargon.

content.practice: Rewrite 'PEBKAC, rebooted, closed' as a professional ticket note.

quiz.p: The first step on any contact is…
With a frustrated user you should…

content.intro: Trust is the currency of IT — handle access and data responsibly.

ul: Use admin access only for the task at hand
Never snoop; least privilege applies to you too

note.text: In the real world: Techs have powerful access — the fastest way to lose a job (and references) is misusing it. Professionalism protects users and you.

p: Know when to say 'I'll find out' rather than guessing, and when to escalate a security concern.

content.practice: Name two ways a tech demonstrates trustworthiness with elevated access.

o: only for the task at hand
quiz.ex: Least privilege applies to techs too.

quiz.p: When you make a mistake you should…

content.intro: Good notes turn one fix into a repeatable solution for the whole team.

ul: What was reported, what you found, what you did
Clear enough for the next tech to continue
Write KB articles for recurring issues
Title by symptom users search for

note.text: In the real world: A well-written KB article you author once can resolve the same issue hundreds of times via self-service — the highest-leverage thing a Tier-1 tech does.

p: Documentation shortens future tickets, enables escalation, and proves your work.

content.practice: Outline the sections of a good KB article for 'Outlook won't open'.

quiz.ex: Anyone should be able to pick it up.

quiz.p: KB articles should be titled by…
A KB article's leverage is that it…

content.intro: How a ticket flows and how to decide what to work first.

ul: New → Assigned → In Progress → Resolved → Closed
Keep status current; add notes at each step

note.text: In the real world: A single exec's laptop vs a whole floor's network down — prioritization keeps you working the highest-impact issue instead of first-in-first-out.

p: Service Level Agreements set response/resolution targets by priority — meet them and communicate.

content.practice: Given a company-wide email outage and one user's font issue, assign priorities and justify.

courses.title: Everyday Support Tasks
courses.description: The bread-and-butter tickets a Tier-1 tech resolves daily — accounts, printing, remote access, email, and browsers.

content.intro: The single most common ticket — done securely.

ul: Reset, require change at next logon
Never send a password over chat/email in the clear
Reset/re-enroll MFA when a device is lost

note.text: In the real world: Attackers call the help desk pretending to be a user to get a reset — identity verification is your front-line security control, not a formality.

p: Encourage SSPR (self-service password reset) to cut volume.

content.practice: List the identity-verification steps before resetting a password.

quiz.p: A reset password should be sent…

content.intro: Printing breaks constantly — know the usual suspects.

ul: Network printer down for all → check printer/IP

p: One user vs everyone? A shared outage is printer/network-side, not the PC.

note.text: In the real world: Half of 'printer broken' tickets are toner, paper, or a stuck queue — check the simple things before deep troubleshooting.

content.practice: A shared printer is offline for everyone — where do you look first?

quiz.p: A stuck print queue is cleared by…

content.intro: Support remote workers and connect to their machines safely.

ul: Always get user consent; announce actions

note.text: In the real world: Test by IP vs name to split 'VPN down' from 'DNS down' — most 'VPN broken' tickets are actually name resolution.

p: Remote sessions are powerful — verify identity and follow policy.

content.practice: A user's VPN connects but internal sites fail — what do you test?

content.intro: Diagnose the most common Outlook/mail complaints.

note.text: In the real world: A message trace answers 'where did it go?' in seconds — quarantined, rejected, or never arrived — instead of guessing.

p: Verify server settings/ports and that the device accepted policy.

content.practice: A user says an external email never arrived — first diagnostic step?

quiz.p: Best first tool for delivery issues…
Missing mail may be caught by…
A corrupt Outlook profile is fixed by…

content.intro: Web-app problems often come down to a few browser basics.

ul: Try incognito / another browser to isolate

note.text: In the real world: 'The website is broken' is often a stale cache or a rogue extension — incognito mode instantly tells you which side the problem is on.

p: If it fails across browsers and machines, it's likely server-side — escalate.

content.practice: A web app fails in Chrome but works in incognito — likely cause?

quiz.p: Incognito working but normal failing suggests…

quiz.ex: A wrong clock breaks TLS validation.

quiz.p: Failing across all browsers/machines is likely…

courses.title: Tier 1: Windows & Accounts
courses.description: The Tier-1 Windows toolkit: troubleshooting, drivers, updates, remote desktop, and permissions.

content.intro: A repeatable approach to common Windows problems.

ul: Safe Mode to rule out drivers/startup
Slow PC → startup apps, disk, malware

note.text: In the real world: Booting into Safe Mode first tells you instantly whether it's a driver/startup problem or something deeper — it saves hours of guessing.

p: Task Manager, Resource Monitor, Reliability History, Event Viewer.

content.practice: List three first checks for a 'slow computer' ticket.

quiz.p: First checks for a slow PC…
Clues to app errors live in…

content.intro: Diagnose hardware and driver issues the Tier-1 way.

ul: Roll back a bad driver update

note.text: In the real world: A device that worked yesterday and fails after an update is almost always a driver — roll it back before deeper troubleshooting.

p: Test the device on another PC / another port to split device vs machine.

content.practice: A webcam stopped working after updates — what's your first move?

quiz.p: A yellow ! in Device Manager means…
A device broken right after an update →

o: a USB found in the lot

content.intro: Keep systems patched and fix update failures.

p: Updates close security holes and fix bugs — a core security control.

ul: Reset Windows Update components if stuck

note.text: In the real world: Unpatched machines are the top target for malware — 'we'll update later' is how ransomware gets in.

p: In business, updates are often managed (WSUS/Intune) — know it's centralized.

content.practice: An update keeps failing at install — list two things to check.

content.intro: Connect to machines remotely to support and administer.

ul: Enable Remote Desktop; it uses port 3389
Only expose over VPN, never open to the internet
Remote-assist tools for user consent sessions

note.text: In the real world: Exposing RDP (3389) directly to the internet is a classic breach vector — always tunnel it through a VPN.

p: Can't connect? Check the service, firewall, IP/name, and permissions.

content.practice: Why should RDP never be exposed directly to the internet?

content.intro: Resolve the access tickets that fill a Tier-1 queue.

ul: Most restrictive of the two wins
Assign access via groups, not individuals

note.text: In the real world: The fastest fix for most access tickets is adding the user to the right security group — resist granting one-off permissions that no one can audit later.

p: Broken inheritance causes surprise denials — check the folder's effective permissions.

content.practice: When Share and NTFS permissions differ, which applies?
